title: 'The best club in the world to be at' - Gvardiol signs new deal
description: Manchester City defender Josko Gvardiol has officially signed a new five-year contract to extend his stay at Etihad Stadium.  The 24-year-old, who joined the club from RB Leipzig in August 2023, has since made 122 appearances and won six trophies under previous manager Pep Guardiola.  Gvardiol contributed two goals and five assists across 25 appearances last season, while also representing Croatia at his second World Cup this summer.
fullText:
Manchester City defender Josko Gvardiol has officially signed a new five-year contract to extend his stay at Etihad Stadium.

The 24-year-old, who joined the club from RB Leipzig in August 2023, has since made 122 appearances and won six trophies under previous manager Pep Guardiola.

Gvardiol contributed two goals and five assists across 25 appearances last season, while also representing Croatia at his second World Cup this summer.

He also played a pivotal role as Manchester City became the first team in English football to secure four consecutive top-flight titles in 2023-24.

"As soon as I knew City wanted to renew my contract, I felt straight away that it was what I wanted," Gvardiol said. "The fans have been unbelievable with me from day one and the club provides absolutely everything for its players.

"It is the best club in the world to be at. I have felt so much love and respect during my three years here, and I don't take that for granted.

"The players we have here are amazing. This is a world-class squad that is young and full of potential.

"I truly believe we will have a lot of success in the coming years."

Director of football Hugo Viana added: "He epitomises what we want in our defenders. He can play in multiple positions, he is quick and strong, and when he attacks he does it superbly.

"He is exceptional, but the way he conducts himself is also very impressive. This young man is determined to be the best he can be - an approach totally aligned with our overall vision."

title: The FA confirm 3 new anti-timewasting rules
description: The FA have confirmed that the International Football Association Board have approved a new goalkeeper injury trial for the 2026/27 Premier League season.Photo by Michael Regan/Getty ImagesThe FA have...
fullText:
The FA have officially announced that English football has received approval from IFAB to trial a new system to cut down on tactical goalkeeper injury timeouts.

For a while, teams have abused the fact that a goalkeeper going down for medical treatment doesn’t have to leave the field of play afterwards. A goalkeeper can go down, disrupt momentum, and give their team time to address things tactically during the break, with no negative consequences.

The trial will introduce such a consequence, requiring the head coach to immediately nominate a player to leave the pitch for a minimum of one minute after the game restarts.

There will be exceptions to the rule, including if the goalkeeper is fouled, if the goalkeeper is bleeding, or if the goalkeeper and an outfield player have collided and both need attention.

But the hope is that this will cut down on potential sporting advantages associated with such stoppages.

The FA add that they will also be introducing a five-second countdown option for match officials to use when they believe players are unfairly delaying a throw-in or goal-kick. The system was used at the World Cup, and it will now be introduced in English football.

Finally, a ten-second limit will be in place for players leaving the pitch when substituted.

The trial will take place across the Premier League, the FA Cup, and the League Cup this season, as well as the upcoming Community Shield match. So it will apply to Arsenal in all competitions except the Champions League.

title: England keeper Hampton extends deal at Chelsea
description: England international Hannah Hampton signs a new two-year deal with Chelsea.
fullText:
England international Hannah Hampton has signed a new two-year deal with Chelsea.

The goalkeeper's contract was set to expire this summer and it was key that Chelsea kept her as part of an effort to bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 campaign.

After joining from Aston Villa in 2023, Hampton has become one of the world's best goalkeepers and cemented her position as first choice for the Lionesses.

The 25-year-old has won five trophies during her time in west London and was a standout performer as England won Euro 2025.

She won the Yashin Trophy for best goalkeeper at the Ballon d'Or awards last year and joins fellow England internationals Lucy Bronze and Aggie Beever-Jones in signing new Chelsea deals this summer.

"I'm really happy," Hampton said. "Chelsea have always been my dream club to play for in England so to be able to extend for another two years is a proud moment.

"When I moved to London from the Midlands, it was my first time moving away from home and everyone at Chelsea made it feel like a home away from home and somewhere I have been able to grow, not only as a player, but as a person.

"I don't want that journey to stop and I want to continue to grow more and learn more as a person. I know there is so much more I can achieve and so much more, we as a team, can achieve.

"I am going to do everything I can to help Chelsea get back to being as successful as we have been in the past."

Hampton was also part of the England squad that won Euro 2022 and reached the 2023 Women's World Cup final.

She helped Chelsea to an unbeaten domestic treble in 2024-25 and has claimed back-to-back Golden Glove awards in the WSL.

Chelsea have gone through a transitional year with several big-name players leaving this summer upon expiration of their contracts.

Striker Sam Kerr, midfielder Guro Reiten and former club captain Millie Bright all left at the end of the season, while several other players remained out of contract.

Hampton's renewal was vital for Chelsea's future plans and there was growing anxiety from the fanbase on whether an agreement had been reached.

She has had a difficult few years in the media, with the release of Mary Earps' autobiography throwing her into the spotlight, but Hampton's quality on the pitch has been clear.

Widely regarded as one of the most talented goalkeepers in the WSL, this season she will hope to reproduce the form she showed during Euro 2025.

title: Former world champion Cordina denies assaulting man, court hears
description: Joe Cordina, 34, was charged in connection with an incident outside a petrol station in February.
fullText:
Former boxing world champion Joe Cordina has denied assaulting a man outside a petrol station, a court has heard.

Cordina, 34, was one of two men charged in connection with an incident in the Cardiff suburb of Pentwyn in February.

He appeared at Cardiff Magistrates' Court on Tuesday and pleaded not guilty to two charges of assault by beating.

Cordina appeared in the dock alongside Jamie O'Brien, 32, from Pentwyn, who has also been charged with assault in connection with the incident.

O'Brien did not enter a plea during the short hearing.

The court previously heard the offences the two men are charged with are alleged to be "against each other".

Nadeem Majid, representing Cordina, said the second charge of assault he faces "emanates from one continued incident".

District Judge Charlotte Murphy granted Cordina unconditional bail until a trial, which was set for 13 October this year.

O'Brien's case was adjourned until 26 August.

Cordina is a former super-featherweight world champion and was due to fight for the WBO lightweight title in the United States on July 4.

However, he revealed in a social media post that his application for a US visa was refused.

title: No. 1 on the Fortune Global 500: Amazon’s Jeff Bezos on how his garage startup became the largest company in the world by revenue
description: As Amazon pours $200 billion into AI this year, Bezos says the company's next act will define the next decade.
fullText:
Jeff Bezos won't pretend he didn't see this day coming. Sure, when he was sitting in his Bellevue, Wash., garage in 1995, at a makeshift desk made from a wooden door slab, he probably wasn't imagining that his nascent online bookshop would grow into the largest company in the world. Instead, he may have been puzzling over how to set up extension cords to keep his computers and servers running without tripping his home's circuit breakers. Or he may have been mulling over changing the name of his tiny startup, then called Cadabra, to Amazon.

What is Amazon's AI strategy and investment plans?

What challenges and criticisms does Amazon currently face?

How did Amazon become the world's largest company?

How has Bezos transitioned from CEO to other ventures?

But three decades later, now that his startup has become an "everything company" that reportedly delivers as many packages as the U.S. Postal Service; now that the Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud business powers a third of the internet; and now that Amazon has topped the Fortune 500 and ascended to the No. 1 spot in the Global 500—making it the biggest company in the world—Bezos admitted to Fortune: "It's not like it's a complete surprise."

And anyhow, Bezos added in April, sitting at that original door-desk in his study in Washington, D.C., bigness was never the point. "I don't want us to take pride in being big," Bezos said. "I want us to take pride in servicing customers. And it turns out, if you service customers really well, that will drive growth."

"Customer obsession" has long been a mantra for the 62-year-old Amazon founder. (In fact, he used the phrase 10 times during our conversation.) And with good reason: It's what propelled the company to the top of Fortune's annual list of the largest companies in the world by revenue, a spot held by Walmart for over a decade. Amazon will likely become the first company to reach $1 trillion in revenue in the next few years.

Bezos, one of the richest people in the world, handed the CEO role to AWS chief Andy Jassy in 2021, but he still serves as Amazon's executive chair, and he's often asked about the company's next big projects. Satellite internet? Advertising solutions? Health care? Yes, yes, and yes.

But the company's biggest venture by far is a bid to own the future of AI. Amazon devoted $131 billion to capital expenditures in 2025 and estimates that it will spend some $200 billion in 2026—largely on AWS and generative AI. In April, Amazon inked a multibillion-dollar deal with Meta, which will use Amazon's Graviton chips to support AI initiatives. It has also partnered with Anthropic, agreeing to invest as much as $25 billion in the AI startup, which will purchase more than $100 billion of Amazon's cloud services.

title: MLS make Lionel Messi exception over punishment rule that left him ‘very upset’ in 2025
description: The MLS have decided to exempt Lionel Messi from the huge punishment that they imposed on him in 2025. With the FIFA World Cup ending just a little over a week ago, many have wondered when Lionel Messi would return to Inter Miami.
fullText:
The MLS have decided to exempt Lionel Messi from the huge punishment that they imposed on him in 2025.

With the FIFA World Cup ending just a little over a week ago, many have wondered when Lionel Messi would return to Inter Miami.

Messi helped lead Argentina to the FIFA World Cup final and has been away from his club side since then as he recovers, which will force him to miss one of the MLS’s landmark events.

Lionel Messi is confirmed to be missing the 2026 MLS All-Star week in Charlotte, North Carolina, as he takes time away from Inter Miami following a grueling FIFA World Cup.

MLS officials confirmed to ESPN that Messi will not receive a one-match suspension for missing the festivities, the standard punishment issued to players.

However, this isn’t a case of Messi receiving preferential treatment as a star player, as the MLS had agreed to let players participating in the FIFA World Cup get some time off to recover.

This is why Messi and Rodrigo de Paul are exempt from the punishment, as a statement from the MLS revealed:

“Prior to the start of the 2026 season, Major League Soccer and the MLS Players Association agreed that upon a player’s exit from the World Cup competition, clubs would have individual conversations with each player to determine the appropriate rest and return to training and competition timeline.

“Consistent with that agreement, Rodrigo De Paul and Lionel Messi will be excused from participating in the 2026 MLS All-Star Game.”

This decision is a stark contrast to last year, when Messi, along with Jordi Alba, received a one-match suspension for missing the event.

This decision was criticized by Miami Heat co-owner Jorge Mas last year, who revealed how upset Messi was over the ‘draconian’ punishment.

“Lionel Messi is very upset, like we all are in the club, with the fact that they won’t be able to play tomorrow night.

“But I think what we have to do as a club is to get together as one, have an attitude that is us against the world… I think that the punishment for the rule is frankly draconian.

“Obviously, it was not a positive reaction [from Messi and Alba]. They want to compete, they want to play games.

“That’s what they’re here for, to play and win. They understand the magnitude of tomorrow night’s game.

“So no, their reaction was exactly as expected of two competitive players who don’t understand the decision, who don’t understand why not attending an exhibition match leads directly to a suspension.”

title: The Iran and Ukraine wars are colliding on the world’s biggest lake. Here’s what to know
description: The Caspian Sea has become the latest region to be sucked into the growing conflict between Iran and its adversaries – not least because it’s a vital artery in the growing relationship between Iran an...
fullText:
The Caspian Sea has become the latest region to be sucked into the growing conflict between Iran and its adversaries – not least because it's a vital artery in the growing relationship between Iran and Russia.

Ukraine at the weekend said its drones had struck two Russian vessels carrying military cargoes in the Caspian, the world's largest inland body of water. It asserted that both had left Iran for a Russian port.

In a post on X Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the targets included "ships that were involved in transporting military cargo from Iran, as well as a warship," subsequently identified by Ukraine's security service as a Russian missile boat.

Iran countered that one of its commercial vessels carrying a cargo of iron had been struck, killing one seafarer and injuring three others.

The ship, which it did not name, was sailing from the Russian port of Astrakhan to Anzali in Iran, which Iranian regional governor Hadi Hagh-Shenas described as "a safe and reliable corridor for commercial exchanges between the two ports."

Tensions escalated further Monday when Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said, "Ukraine's dangerous adventurism will certainly not go unanswered by us." Meanwhile, Ukraine's Chargé d'Affaires in Tehran was summoned to the foreign ministry over the incident.

The recriminations reflect the growing importance of the Caspian, which is bordered by five countries, including Iran and Russia. With the blockade of Iranian ports in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, the Caspian has taken on new significance as a trade route.

The Caspian can help Iran towards "a diversified trade strategy, especially if Iran promotes trade with Russia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, China via rail, and, indirectly, Eastern Europe," according to Bijan Khajehpour, managing partner of Vienna-based Eurasian Nexus Partners, a consulting firm.

It is "a strategic complement rather than a substitute for Iran's existing maritime access through the southern waters," Khajehpour told CNN.

Russian grain and steel are among the cargoes that cross the Caspian. Iran has developed several significant ports on the sea, among them Anzali. Oil and gas from Kazakhstan are transported from the Caspian to a hub on the Black Sea.

For Russia, the Caspian is an important conduit to central Asia and Iran – and a critical route in its expanding strategic partnership with Tehran, one that has a military component as well as Russia's role in Iran's civilian nuclear program and oil exploration in Iran.

"The recent blockade by the US (of Iranian ports) has underlined the strategic value of the Caspian Sea route" says Khajehpour. It is also less vulnerable to international sanctions because it is landlocked and largely controlled by Iran, Russia and neighboring states beyond Western naval reach.

The Caspian has become a passageway for the growing military links between Moscow and Tehran. Iran and Russia have a broad strategic agreement covering economic and military collaboration, although it is not a mutual defense pact.

Russia received its first batches of Iranian Shahed attack drones via the Caspian early in its war with Ukraine and has since produced new versions of the drones in plants on Russian soil.

The Caspian route linking Iran's northern ports to the Russian port of Astrakhan has been targeted by Ukraine before. Last August a cargo ship – the Port Olya 4 – was destroyed while reportedly loaded with Shahed-136 drone components and Iranian munitions.

In 2024, CNN reported that a Russian cargo ship suspected of carrying Iranian ballistic missiles for Moscow's war against Ukraine was seen at a Russian port on the Caspian Sea. The US Treasury department assessed that the Russian Ministry of Defense had "used the vessel Port Olya-3 to transport CRBMs (close-range ballistic missiles) from Iran to Russia."

Then-US Secretary of State Antony Blinken said Washington believed the Russian military had received shipments of Iranian Fatah-360 ballistic missiles and would "likely use them within weeks in Ukraine against Ukrainians."

At the same time, the US National Security Council warned of the deepening military cooperation between Iran and Russia. Spokesperson Sean Savett told CNN back then that "any transfer of Iranian ballistic missiles to Russia would represent a dramatic escalation in Iran's support" for the Kremlin in its invasion of Ukraine.

Iran denied it was providing military assistance to Russia at that time.

Ukraine's drone attacks on vessels and energy infrastructure in the Caspian at the weekend are a demonstration of its growing long-range capabilities and its goal of damaging the industries that support Russia's war effort.

It's also a recognition that Iran – like North Korea – plays a significant role in supplying Russia with weapons.

And above all, it's astute timing from the Ukrainians, with Zelensky traveling to Washington this week to meet with President Donald Trump. Besides the Caspian strikes, Zelensky has said that according to Ukrainian intelligence Russia has provided satellite data to Iran to carry out attacks on US facilities in the Middle East.

The message: we are on the same side.

title: Meditate, pray or watch football instead of spreading hate - Infantino
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino tells critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about him and the World Cup.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino has told critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about his leadership, the governing body and the World Cup.

In a 15-slide post on his personal Instagram account - reposted to Fifa's eight million followers - Infantino addressed "those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens" to affirm his belief that, while they were "busy planting seeds of hate", Fifa was delivering the "greatest event on earth".

He said the World Cup "celebrated humanity at its best", adding that the 2026 tournament had "100% safety and security, only joy and happiness".

Infantino downplayed several of the tournament's high-profile controversies and hailed the involvement of Iran, who featured at the World Cup despite their ongoing conflict with co-hosts the United States, as a success.

He said Fifa "worked tirelessly to unite two countries at war", with Iran entering the country "without incident or conflict".

His comments are in stark contradiction to those of Iran's head coach Amir Ghalenoei, who said his team were the "most oppressed" at the World Cup.

Infantino's 'time is up' with Fifa - La Liga boss

The country that doesn't play football... yet

Iran faced visa delays, "integral" members of their backroom staff were denied entry to the US and fans had their allocation of tickets revoked, while Iran also had to move their training base from Tucson, Arizona to Tijuana, Mexico following a multitude of logistical issues in the build up to the tournament.

They later also encountered restrictions on their movements as they travelled between their training base and group matches in Los Angeles and Seattle.

Such issues were not unique to Iran, with fans from Haiti, Senegal, and Ivory Coast impacted by travel bans imposed by the Trump administration, while Somali referee Omar Artan was denied entry to the US - despite holding a diplomatic passport and a single entry US visa - because of his "association with suspected members of terror organisations".

Infantino wrote: "You mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world. Because football unites the world, and it was impressively demonstrated this summer."

Doubling down on the tournament's safety, Infantino said there were "zero incidents, zero violence, just joy, emotions, happiness, unity, and togetherness".

However, Fifa is investigating Argentina's actions after players and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain's players after losing the World Cup final. It is also investigating allegations of racist abuse towards American social media influencer IShowSpeed, while supporters were arrested at multiple matches - including following England's semi-final against Argentina in Atlanta.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials were also controversially present at World Cup stadiums.

Infantino also addressed criticism surrounding the standard of officiating at the tournament, in particular concerns about political interference after USA forward Folarin Balogun was made available for their last-16 tie when his one-match ban was suspended by Fifa - following the intervention of US President Donald Trump.

Of the 191 other red cards shown at a men's World Cup, only one other player has escaped a suspension.

Uefa said the decision had "crossed a red line", labelling it "unprecedented, incomprehensible, and unjustifiable", while the Norwegian Football Federation is considering filing a formal complaint to Fifa's ethics committee.

Infantino, however, argued that such decisions are not out of the ordinary, claiming similar rulings are "routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide".

He added: "It's curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticising."

The International Olympic Committee has said it will not investigate Infantino for any possible breaches of political neutrality, stating the complaint levelled by human rights campaign group FairSquare falls outside the jurisdiction of its ethics commission.

Infantino's advice to his opponents was "to show some love" and "respect" to a tournament where "people came together as families, as fans, as one".

"To everyone who missed our beautiful game, the emotions, the celebrations, the laughter, the crying, the deception and the joy. To all of you who missed watching kids, babies, grandparents and parents come together for the beautiful game... sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all," Infantino wrote.

"While they celebrated, you were busy planting seeds of hate. Our world needs love, not hate; tolerance, not division; celebration, not mourning.

"To those spending their time and energy hating us, please take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray or watch a football match and truly observe the faces, the eyes, the emotions.

"Because only our beautiful game can deliver such an extraordinary show, a show where everyone becomes one and reconnects as humans.

"I am incredibly proud, as Fifa President, to have contributed, even a little, to this show. It's a great feeling."

It may be that Infantino's astonishing outburst reflects a genuine grievance he feels about some of the criticism Fifa has faced over its handling of the World Cup. It appears he does not believe the governing body has received enough credit for organising a tournament that enjoyed record ticket sales, entertained many millions, and successfully delivered a huge security operation, despite the tense geopolitical landscape. It also arguably conveys a high degree of confidence in his position and chances of re-election next year, that he feels he can be so defiant.

But for many, turning on his critics in such a fashion, and portraying them as negative, biased and unfair 'haters', risks reinforcing an impression that Fifa is unable or unwilling to handle legitimate scrutiny, and is out of touch.

The reality is that a host of controversies made such scrutiny inevitable; the issues related to US visa policies, which undermined claims that it would be the most welcoming tournament ever. The unprecedented costs facing fans. The outcry over Fifa's suspension of Folarin Balogun's ban after lobbying by US President Trump, leading to concerns over political interference (regardless of Fifa's denials). The introduction of innovations such as hydration breaks and a 27 minute long half-time show for the final. And the environmental impact of the biggest and longest World Cup ever.

Infantino held a media conference on the eve of the tournament - his first for three years - when he told his critics to "chill & relax". Maybe, if he had conducted another one after the event began or once it ended, he could have addressed some of the issues it raised sooner, and not responded in a way that many will see as further evidence of a siege mentality.

title: 'Medal dream didn't come true but my other dream is fighting brain cancer'
description: Little over two years ago, Archie Goodburn's world fell apart when he was diagnosed with brain cancer - he has just competed in a Commonwealth Games final.
fullText:
Little over two years ago, Archie Goodburn's world fell apart.

The Scottish 50m breaststroke record holder was dreaming of the Paris Olympics when he checked his phone at the end of another gruelling pool session.

His training had been hindered a little in recent weeks by some odd issues. Seizures. Numbness on his left side. A feeling of deja-vu.

Test had been done and his scan results were due. So when he dried off and saw a missed call on his phone, he called back. The news that followed was devastating.

Goodburn was told he had brain cancer. He was 22 years old.

Further investigation, including biopsy surgery, revealed three 'low grade' tumours. Inoperable and unable to be removed given how they had spread through his brain.

The reality, he was told, was that he might not see his 40s.

So when Goodburn - now 25 - walked out to perhaps the loudest ovation of the week at Tollcross on Monday to compete in a Commonwealth Games final, a malestrom of emotions must have been coursing though him.

After qualifying on Sunday, tears fell. The magnitude of what had happened, of what he is doing, hit home. But by the time he stepped on the blocks for the final, the competitor had returned.

"Last night, I was so overcome to have achieved that primary goal of making the final. Then over the next 24 hours, you look for more," he told BBC Sport Scotland.

The brain cancer patient targeting Commonwealth medal this summer

The Commonwealth Games swimmer who might not see 40

MacInnes overcomes nerves to win swimming silver

The attitude is understandable. Goodburn is - astonishingly - in the best shape of his life in swimming terms. He lowered the national record to 27.12 seconds in February and qualified fifth fastest for this.

New treatments - which he fought hard to be given access to - have slowed the growth of his tumours, and he recently graduated from Edinburgh University with a first in chemical engineering.

Ultimately, he finished joint seventh - "joint last" as he put it - and missed out on the 50m breaststroke medal he craved.

But this race and this week has been about so much more than podiums and plaudits for this remarkable young man from Edinburgh, who continues to fight not only his own brain cancer, but the impact of the disease on others.

"It's pretty indescribable," he told BBC Sport Scotland when asked what the past 24 hours have been like. "Usually the words flow easily, but I'm finding myself quite speechless.

"I was really trying to soak it up, because I didn't feel like I really got much of a chance to do that after the semi. And the experience was everything I dreamed of and more. But the time, unfortunately, wasn't there."

These Games - and this summer - have been such a focus for Goodburn amid the darkness of the past two years, and he spoke afterwards about being eager to watch back the race and pore over his data as many athletes would.

He also talked about the support of his family and girlfriend Ciara Schlosshan, who competed for Scotland in the 100m butterfly just five minutes before he did.

But not many swimmers - standing wrapped in a towel, with goggles strapped to their head - would talk so passionately and eruditely about ensuring brain cancer research is properly resourced.

Team-mate Duncan Scott called Goodburn "inspirational" - and no wonder.

"I was thinking today - the goal was to make the final, and the dream was to win a medal," Goodburn said.

"That dream didn't come true, but one of my other dreams is that we see a future where brain cancer isn't the biggest killer of patients under 40.

"I advocate to try and extend my own life, but also for the other young patients and adults going through what I'm going through.

"With everything that's going on with my health, it's been difficult to think 'why am I here? Am I here to advocate as a patient advocate, or am I here to just be a professional athlete?' And it's kind of turned into a bit of both.

"I wonder how I'm going to feel off the back of this. But I know that I'm going to have memories to last a lifetime."

title: Gianni Infantino Lashes Out at World Cup Critics
description: The FIFA president ripped the media in an Instagram post.
fullText:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino posted a 15-slide message directed at people “busy planting seeds of hate” on Instagram on Sunday night, claiming the World Cup went off without incident.

Infantino’s Sunday night missive began: “To everyone who missed our beautiful game…sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all.” He went on to further single out people “behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours.”

The post was filled with jarring and inaccurate claims; he wrote that the World Cup saw “zero incidents, zero hostility, zero violence, just joy, emotions, happiness, unity, and togetherness.”

Four people died during celebrations in Mexico City after Mexico beat Ecuador in the round of 32. South African midfielder Jayden Adams was found dead in Cape Town after returning from the tournament, and police are investigating a cause of death.

FIFA did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the inaccuracies or what prompted Infantino’s post.

Even and especially at its best, the World Cup—as always—stirred up hostility and political tensions. Argentine fans in Atlanta were captured on video fighting with one another on the night before the match, and with England fans after the semifinal win. The match reignited historic claims from the Argentine government, players, and fans against Great Britain over the Falkland Islands, including with an on-pitch demonstration by the players. In the U.K., more domestic abuse incidents were reported during the tournament than the past two World Cups and Euros.

Infantino also wrote that “Iran entered the United States without incident or conflict.” Iran’s coach, though, said his side was “perhaps the most oppressed” team in the tournament after the quick trip from Tijuana to Los Angeles took five hours with security screenings, then the team would need to return immediately after the match. Iran saw 11 federation members and team staffers denied entry into the U.S., including federation president Mehdi Taj.

The Iranian federation also said it would file a complaint to FIFA for denying its request to travel two days in advance of its match against Belgium.

Infantino wrote that “Football is bigger than hate and discrimination.” Multiple incidents of racist abuse occurred during the World Cup. Most notably, a Paraguayan senator called Kylian Mbappé a “colonised Cameroonian,” to which the French captain called her “a despicable woman and unworthy of your position.”

Infantino said the World Cup’s haters “mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world.”

The most high profile visa cases include that of Somali referee Omar Artan, denied entry into the U.S. over alleged “association with suspected members of terrorist organizations,” and Ghana midfielder Thomas Partey, who was not allowed into Canada for matches due to ongoing rape charges.

And fans from Haiti, Iran, Senegal, and Ivory Coast were simply banned from entering the United States under blanket Trump administration policy; others were subject to a $15,000 bond that deterred many from coming. (FIFA celebrated that it got the U.S. to waive this requirement, but that only applied to a certain subset of fans who had already purchased tickets and opted into an expedited visa process.)

Infantino did not mention Folarin Balogun’s red card or its subsequent suspension directly, but he was still defensive about the notorious incident.

“Indeed, ‘arguable’ referees’ decisions or ‘strange’ disciplinary rulings such as for instance potentially mistaken red or yellow cards or subsequent decisions not to ban players in certain situations are routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide,” Infantino wrote. “It’s curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticising.”

European leaders had blasted FIFA’s handlingof Balogun’s red card to the point where UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin—whose organization called the red card reversal an “unprecedented, incomprehensible and unjustifiable decision”—boycotted the tournament final. (Some European leagues do review red cards after games, which is not generally FIFA protocol.)

Infantino has not taken questions from reporters since a press conference before the opening match in Mexico City on June 10.

There, Infantino was also defensive and vague, saying, “We try to do our best” on a number of issues like Iran, high ticket prices, and visa restrictions. After initially telling people to “chill, relax,” Infantino later clarified that he meant “to trust us that we are working behind the scenes.”

He was more aggressive on Sunday night.

“To those spending their time and energy hating us, please take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray, or watch a football match and truly observe the faces, the eyes, the emotions,” Infantino wrote. “To the pens and papers, to all the screens, may you find love and peace where the people behind you couldn’t.

“May you find peace; we at FIFA have found ours and we deliver it, by delivering the most outstanding FIFA World Cup.”

Also on Sunday night, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D., MD) sent Infantino a letter asking for a list of any money or gifts exchanged between FIFA and anyone related to President Trump, and visitor logs at the governing body’s Miami and New York offices. FIFA houses its New York office in Trump Tower. The Athletic first reported news of the letter.

Raskin also asked Infantino to appear before the House Judiciary Committee, of which he is the ranking member.

fullText:
The US Open introduced a $1 million top prize in 2025 to attract some of the world’s top players to its mixed doubles tournament.

The second year of the new prize format features a stacked lineup with a pairing of Novak Djokovic and Aryana Sabalenka at the top of the marquee. The US Open announced the pairing Monday as part of the initial list of entrants to the tournament. More are yet to be announced, as are the matchups.

Djokovic is a 24-time Grand Slam champion and four-time singles winner at the US Open. Sabalenka is the world No. 1, a four-time Grand Slam winner and the two-time reigning US Open champion in singles. They’ll be joined be other high-profiles singles players in the mixed doubles draw.

Six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Świątek will join Casper Ruud again after the pairing advanced to the final of last year’s mixed doubles tournament. Other standout pairings include Jessica Pegula and Jack Draper, Elena Rybakina and Taylor Fritz, Leylah Fernandez and Frances Tiafoe and Naomi Osaka and Kei Nishikori.

Mixed doubles specialists Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori will also return in search of their third consecutive US Open title. The new format drew criticism last year for prioritizing big-name singles players over traditional mixed doubles specialists like Errani and Vavassori. But Errani and Vavassori prevailed over the field and defeated Świątek and Ruud in the final to capture the third of their four mixed doubles Grand Slam titles.

Mixed doubles play is scheduled to start on Aug 24, and the final is scheduled for Aug 26. The first round of the US Open singles draw is scheduled to start on Aug. 30.

fullText:
BEIJING, July 27 (Reuters) - Profits at China's industrial firms grew at a solid, though slower, pace as resilient exports helped cushion sluggish domestic demand, highlighting ‌the economy's uneven recovery despite policymakers' efforts to spur consumption.

Exports and industrial production ‌have done much of the heavy lifting for the world's second-largest economy. Persistent weakness in consumption and the ​property sector, however, helped drag second-quarter growth to its slowest pace in more than three years, keeping calls alive for further policy support to address economic imbalances.

Industrial profit growth eased to 15.1% in June from 21.1% in May, while first-half profits rose 18.7% from a ‌year earlier, compared with an ⁠18.8% increase in the January-to-May period, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed on Monday.

"If this recovery can be sustained, it will ⁠be a good sign for the rest of the economy, as a return of profits growth could give companies room to resume wage growth," said Lynn Song, chief economist of Greater ​China at ​ING.

The figures add to evidence of a two-speed ​recovery in the world's second-largest economy, ‌where manufacturers have benefited from robust overseas demand, while sectors tied to domestic spending continue to struggle.

"The external environment remains complex and international commodity prices uncertain," NBS statistician Yu Weining said. "Industrial firms also face weak demand and cash flow pressures."

Underlining strains in the domestic market, automobile manufacturing profits fell 19.5% in the first half of the year, NBS ‌data showed, as car sales declined for a ninth ​consecutive month in June.

Market reaction was muted with ​Chinese stocks and the yuan slightly ​firmer following the data.

Attention is now turning to the Communist Party's Politburo ‌meeting at the end of July, ​a key policy-setting gathering ​where investors will look for signals on additional support measures.

Expectations for a broad-based stimulus package have been tempered, however, by resilient exports and Beijing's preference for targeted ​easing.

title: England netball team returns to winning ways
description: England bounce back from a difficult loss to world number one side Australia with a 73-38 victory over Malawi at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
fullText:
England bounced back from a difficult loss to world number one side Australia with a 73-38 victory over Malawi at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

There was no hangover from the 66-47 loss to Australia as England cruised into a 18-9 lead in the first quarter.

England consistently kept their advantage throughout before stepping it up in the final quarter to allow Malawi just five points to the Roses' 18.

Goal shooter Eleanor Cardwell proved to be an influential substitution, scoring all of her 21 shots following her introduction in the second half.

"After yesterday's loss, we've definitely turned things around and fixed some of the things we got wrong," said vice-captain Amy Carter.

"At the start of a tournament, a loss isn't actually a bad thing to have. In the last 24 hours, we've looked at video, righted some of the wrongs, connected as a group, had a games night and just spent time together as team-mates.

"We didn't get too bogged down by it because we've got to look forward."

The Roses are third in Pool A behind reigning champions Australia and South Africa.

They will next face Tonga on Wednesday at 16:00 BST before playing South Africa - their rivals for a place in the semi-finals - on Thursday at 21:00 BST.

England are looking to regain the gold they won in 2018 but have had a rocky preparation for the tournament.

Jess Thirlby stepped down as head coach in March for family reasons, leaving assistant Anna Stembridge in interim charge, while injuries to Helen Housby and Natalie Metcalf mean 10 of the Roses' 12-player squad have made their Commonwealth debuts in Glasgow.

Tonga recorded their first ever Commonwealth Games win as they beat Northern Ireland 58-52 in an enthralling game at the Hydro.

After two defeats from their first two games, Tonga started well on Monday and led 15-11 after a clinical first quarter.

It was a more competitive second quarter as the Warriors, who had also suffered two losses from their first two games, fought back but they still trailed 31-26 at the half-time break.

Tonga pulled away again in the third period to lead 45-37 and closed out the victory despite Northern Ireland outscoring them in the final quarter.

The result leaves Northern Ireland bottom of Pool A before a tough game against South Africa on Tuesday at 14:00.

fullText:
The 2026 World Cup is over, and instead of focusing on the joys of the event, FIFA President Gianni Infantino took a moment to call out its critics in one of his first comments since the final.

In a lengthy social-media post, Infantino ripped critics who he accused of “spreading hate” during the 2026 World Cup.

Infantino’s statement immediately begins with him calling out those who “missed our beautiful game.”

“To all of you who missed watching kids, babies, grandparents, and parents come together for the beautiful game, I say sorry that the matches are now over and sorry that you missed all that joy and togetherness.

“Sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all.”

From there, Infantino appeared to take a shot at journalists covering the 2026 World Cup:

“To those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours, I want to say that while you are sitting behind, we at FIFA are on the front lines organising, working hard, and delivering the best show in the world.

“While you hide, we are exploring the streets of Canada, Mexico, and the United States, talking with fans, engaging with people, and ensuring everyone’s safety.

Infantino then went on to thank the host countries for providing a welcoming atmosphere during games before once again condemning critics of the event.

“While they celebrated, you were busy planting seeds of hate.

“Our world needs love, not hate; tolerance, not division; celebration, not mourning.

“While you spread hatred, we worked tirelessly to unite two countries at war.

“Iran entered the United States without incident or conflict.”

“Football is about unity, not division.

Football is bigger than hate and discrimination.”

In the post, Infantino also addressed “‘arguable’ referees’ decisions.”

“Indeed, ‘arguable’ referees’ decisions or ‘strange’ disciplinary rulings such as for instance potentially mistaken red or yellow cards or subsequent decisions not to ban players in certain situations are routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide.

“It’s curious that the same countries employing these practices are the onces criticising.”

He then ended the statement with, “Much love to all.”

Infantino’s post is … a curious way to address what, on many levels, was a successful World Cup. While the event was subject to plenty of criticism, some due to President Donald Trump’s involvement and the United States’ immigration policies, some due to potential mishandling of punishments handed out during games, particularly one involving USMNT striker Folarin Balogun, there was a lot to celebrate from the actual event.

Videos of opposing fans being embraced and celebrated by United States citizens were among the best part of the 2026 World Cup. When the games actually began, a record number of fans from the U.S. tuned in.

That should have given Infantino plenty to celebrate. Instead, he — for whatever reason — decided to focus on all the potential negatives surrounding the event.

fullText:
The debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyes

The wilds of the sub-Arctic north: towering pine trees, flashes of psychedelic-yellow lichen, and a sun that never wholly sets during the summer months. This land is gorgeous, yes, but also unforgiving, yet in Haex (pronounced “hex”) you have an unusual tool at your disposal to make it a little more hospitable: a cube that fits snugly in the palm of your hand out of which grows a plant. You plant this so-called Seed in the earth and – voilà – the world around you transforms: new vegetation and topography but also narrative threads to follow, and, naturally, enemies. Wield these small-but-mighty kernels of change at your own peril.

“Your adventure and your world is player-shaped,” says Haex’s creative director Tobias Nyman. He explains that everyone starts a campaign with a unique, procedurally generated world. Each Seed then contains further procedural data that causes it to terraform before your eyes. “You change the world as you go,” he says. “It becomes even more unique.”

The singularity of each game world is crucial for keeping not just you but other players on their toes. That’s another of Haex’s wrinkles: it is an online co-operative game, meaning your friends may join you on this ever-transforming survivalist adventure.

Teaming up, you play as a group of research scientists sent to investigate an anomaly in the rugged Scandinavian landscape. You come across odd, shapeshifting objects and beasts: for example, an ash-grey humanoid creature with spikes protruding from its face that would make even Pinhead from Hellraiser wince; also, a sentient wall so supermassive that it scrapes the clouds. There is a further layer to these spatial and, perhaps, alien mysteries: an unknown language of arcane sigils that must be decoded.

Nyman talks effusively of influences: sci-fi movies such as Annihilation and Arrival (as is clear from the trailer); the weird fiction thrillers of author Jeff VanderMeer, too. Unexpectedly, the creative director cites the niche music genre known as cosmic black metal as a touchstone. “There is the wild, grim, frostbitten north, an extraterrestrial entity and a thing that traverses the mist,” says Nyman, hinting at a shared emotional effect between his beloved music genre and the game: a mingling of dread and awe, and of seeking transcendence in nature.

Nyman co-founded Haex’s studio Dead Astronauts (another nod to VanderMeer), in 2024, having previously worked at Ubisoft Massive, where he helped make recent open-world blockbusters, Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora and Star Wars Outlaws. Yet where those titles’ settings are gorgeous and gigantic (“monumental,” stresses Nyman), they are also somewhat static. By contrast, Haex’s game world is more dynamic, and it is being made by just 12 developers. The theory is that its morphing, geo-engineered space should foster more fluid, interesting experiences, despite Haex’s focus on somewhat familiar-feeling shooting and survival mechanics.

Taking the leap to independence has also enabled Nyman to make a game that is more personal to him. As a youngster, he split his time between Stockholm and the far north of Sweden. He recalls looking up at the night sky blanketed with constellations as his father explained Einstein’s theory of relativity. Another memory: gazing out at an expansive crop of cloudberries – a “field of gold,” says Nyman, by virtue of the small fruit’s colour. What has stuck with him most, however, is the region’s silence – a silence so great that it was “almost screaming at me”, he says. That feels like an apt summation of Haex’s aims: an experience that is miraculous and malicious; a setting that is beautiful yet can feel as if it is bearing down on you with cruel intensity.

title: Robertson receives first Scotland call-up as Ihsan & Jones return

Lyle Robertson has received a first senior Scotland call-up for August's ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 series against Canada and the United Arab Emirates.

Falkland's Robertson is one of three changes to the squad that toured Nepal in May, with Zainullah Ihsan and Michael Jones also returning.

title: Second again - why has Scheffler stopped winning?
description: World number one Scottie Scheffler has not won a tournament since January, but what's the reason?
fullText:
It has been six months since world number one Scottie Scheffler won a golf tournament.

Given he earned 14 victories over the previous two seasons, it is a drought few could have conceived when he triumphed at the American Express Open on 27 January 2026.

The four majors have passed without a Scheffler victory - he won both the US PGA Championship and The Open in 2025 - while two weeks ago he missed his first cut in 78 events, ending the longest unbroken streak on the PGA Tour.

On Sunday, he was runner-up in Minnesota to PGA Tour rookie Jackson Koivun.

So is the world's best player past his peak?

Was it mere hyperbole to compare him favourably with Tiger Woods when he was racking up the victories on tour?

Or does his consistency suggest the floodgates are about to re-open?

Woods comparisons continue after Scheffler wins again

How 'Tiger-like' Scheffler is conquering golf

At the top of his powers, Scheffler, 30, is a front-running machine.

Of his 20 victories on tour, 75% have come when he has held the lead going into the final round, albeit his most recent three victories have been when trailing after 54 holes.

This season however, he has not even been joint leader after the third round and therefore always been chasing on a Sunday.

Take the 3M Open this weekend. He shot an eight-under 63 to finish second behind exciting new talent Koivun, but was still three shots back.

Twice in 2026 he has lost in a play-off, to Matt Fitzpatrick and Viktor Hovland. Both times Scheffler trailed going into round four and duly reeled in the leader, only to fall short on the extra hole.

Early in his career, Scheffler coughed up the lead after 54 holes a number of times, including when leading Rory McIlroy by six shots at the Tour Championship in 2022.

Since then, when in front with 18 to play, he has ruthlessly converted. This season, he has not given himself that chance.

Failing to put everything together at once?

At his best, there is an inevitability to Scheffler winning - but over the course of any tournament, a dip in one element can cost him.

For instance, The Open at Royal Birkdale was won brilliantly by New Zealand's Ryan Fox but, if Scheffler's putter had worked during the week, he would have reclaimed the title he took at Royal Portrush last year.

In his second round alone, he missed seven birdie putts from 15 feet or less - four inside 10 feet - and was ranked 60th in the field on the greens.

It is an Achilles' heel that has dogged Scheffler before, but the PGA Tour has him as fifth-best putter, external on tour in 2026 - so it is certainly not a problem every week.

Or perhaps slow starts are costing him. On nine occasions this season, including at the Masters and the US Open, he has begun with a round of 70 or over, leaving himself playing catch-up for the rest of the tournament.

A glance at Scheffler's record shows metronomic consistency across all facets of his game.

Winning a golf tournament is just really, really hard to do.

How Fox kept cool at baked Birkdale to win The Open

Winning does not matter to him?

Before The Open, Scheffler doubled down on previous comments he had made about there being "more to life than playing golf".

Despite being ranked as the world's best player for more than three years, the Texan told reporters the thought of making history "just isn't that important".

A devout Christian and now with two young children, Scheffler has made it clear he would happily walk away from the game if it harmed his family life.

However, before speculating that such a perspective would harm his competitive edge, it is worth evaluating the on-course demeanour of a player who is expressive when his game is not going as well as he would like.

Any suggestion Scheffler does not care about winning would be dismissed within seconds by his caddie Ted Scott, who said earlier this year:, external "If Scheffler was playing a nine-year-old girl in ping pong, he would want to beat her 21-nothing!"

If wins are the only currency, both Matt Fitzpatrick and Cameron Young have three on tour this season, while Wyndham Clark has a regular victory and a US Open.

But a glance at the FedEx Cup's season-long rankings reassert Scheffler's dominance.

Players are awarded points for where they finish in a tournament - and Scheffler has 795 more than Fitzpatrick in second.

That is because even though he has not win since January, he has done everything but.

Sunday's second place at the 3M Open was his fifth runners-up finish - only the second golfer in 40 years to have at least five second places in a season on the PGA Tour.

He has also finished third on two occasions, and in the top five 11 times across 17 starts in 2026. It is a body of work that dwarfs anything put together by his rivals.

"I think I've been really close to winning some tournaments and that can be frustrating," Scheffler said before the Scottish Open.

"At the same time, I've had some good results - a fourth and a second are not bad results by any means. Margins in golf are really small and I just keep trying to do my best."

The lack of wins has not prevented him stretching his lead at the top of the Official World Golf rankings, external either.

In fact, the distance between him and second-placed Rory McIlroy is equivalent to between McIlroy and America's Matt McCarty (in 67th).

Scheffler has been world number one since 21 May 2023 - nearly 166 weeks. Woods' unbroken record stands at 281 weeks, between June 2005 and October 2010.

That intimidating record is still more than two years off for Scheffler, but current evidence suggests knocking him off top spot will be extraordinarily difficult.

title: Infantino tells Fifa critics to 'meditate, pray or watch football'
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino tells critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about him and the World Cup.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino has told critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about his leadership, the governing body and the World Cup.

In a 15-slide post on his personal Instagram account - reposted to Fifa's eight million followers - Infantino addressed "those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens" to affirm his belief that, while they were "busy planting seeds of hate", Fifa was delivering the "greatest event on earth".

He said the World Cup "celebrated humanity at its best", adding that the 2026 tournament had "100% safety and security, only joy and happiness".

Infantino downplayed several of the tournament's high-profile controversies and hailed the involvement of Iran, who featured at the World Cup despite their ongoing conflict with co-hosts the United States, as a success.

He said Fifa "worked tirelessly to unite two countries at war", with Iran entering the country "without incident or conflict".

His comments are in stark contradiction to those of Iran's head coach Amir Ghalenoei, who said his team were the "most oppressed" at the World Cup.

Infantino's 'time is up' with Fifa - La Liga boss

The country that doesn't play football... yet

Iran faced visa delays, "integral" members of their backroom staff were denied entry to the US and fans had their allocation of tickets revoked, while Iran also had to move their training base from Tucson, Arizona to Tijuana, Mexico following a multitude of logistical issues in the build up to the tournament.

They later also encountered restrictions on their movements as they travelled between their training base and group matches in Los Angeles and Seattle.

Such issues were not unique to Iran, with fans from Haiti, Senegal, and Ivory Coast impacted by travel bans imposed by the Trump administration, while Somali referee Omar Artan was denied entry to the US - despite holding a diplomatic passport and a single entry US visa - because of his "association with suspected members of terror organisations".

Infantino wrote: "You mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world. Because football unites the world, and it was impressively demonstrated this summer."

Doubling down on the tournament's safety, Infantino said there were "zero incidents, zero violence, just joy, emotions, happiness, unity, and togetherness".

However, Fifa is investigating Argentina's actions after players and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain's players after losing the World Cup final. It is also investigating allegations of racist abuse towards American social media influencer IShowSpeed, while supporters were arrested at multiple matches - including following England's semi-final against Argentina in Atlanta.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials were also controversially present at World Cup stadiums.

Infantino also addressed criticism surrounding the standard of officiating at the tournament, in particular concerns about political interference after USA forward Folarin Balogun was made available for their last-16 tie when his one-match ban was suspended by Fifa - following the intervention of US President Donald Trump.

Of the 191 other red cards shown at a men's World Cup, only one other player has escaped a suspension.

Uefa said the decision had "crossed a red line", labelling it "unprecedented, incomprehensible, and unjustifiable", while the Norwegian Football Federation is considering filing a formal complaint to Fifa's ethics committee.

Infantino, however, argued that such decisions are not out of the ordinary, claiming similar rulings are "routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide".

He added: "It's curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticising."

The International Olympic Committee has said it will not investigate Infantino for any possible breaches of political neutrality, stating the complaint levelled by human rights campaign group FairSquare falls outside the jurisdiction of its ethics commission.

Infantino's advice to his opponents was "to show some love" and "respect" to a tournament where "people came together as families, as fans, as one".

"To everyone who missed our beautiful game, the emotions, the celebrations, the laughter, the crying, the deception and the joy. To all of you who missed watching kids, babies, grandparents and parents come together for the beautiful game... sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all," Infantino wrote.

"While they celebrated, you were busy planting seeds of hate. Our world needs love, not hate; tolerance, not division; celebration, not mourning.

"To those spending their time and energy hating us, please take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray or watch a football match and truly observe the faces, the eyes, the emotions.

"Because only our beautiful game can deliver such an extraordinary show, a show where everyone becomes one and reconnects as humans.

"I am incredibly proud, as Fifa President, to have contributed, even a little, to this show. It's a great feeling."

title: 9️⃣ players to watch as the 2026 MLS Season returns
description: The 2026 World Cup is over, and we bring our attention back to Major League Soccer as we kick off the second half of the season. Here are some of the stars and breakout candidates who could shape the ...
fullText:
The 2026 World Cup is over, and we bring our attention back to Major League Soccer as we kick off the second half of the season.

Here are some of the stars and breakout candidates who could shape the second half of the season.

Inter Miami vs. Columbus on August 1 at 7:30pm ET. Watch live on Apple TV

New York Red Bull vs. Orlando City on August 1 at 7:30pm ET. Watch live on Apple TV

Chicago vs. Charlotte on August 1 at 8:30pm ET. Watch live on Apple TV

📸 Charlotte Wilson - 2026 Getty Images

One of the breakout stars in the West was tipped to perform highly at the World Cup, and with his former USMNT head coach-for-a-father watching, he did!

Midfielder Sebastian Berhalter impressed under Mauricio Pochettino, notably featuring in all five World Cup games and registering a goal plus an assist against Turkiye. That made him the first American in the modern era to record one goal and one assist in a World Cup match.

He already has 10 combined goals and assists in 14 MLS appearances this season, something he'll look to build on after gaining some confidence seeing his stock rise.

One of the biggest stories following the resumption of the MLS season is Inter Miami's signing of Casemiro. The five-time Champions League winner arrives in South Florida as another marquee addition to a star-studded squad, with hopes of helping Miami strengthen their push for MLS Cup.

The Brazilian could well make his debut this weekend after completing his move late last week, bringing a wealth of experience and winning mentality to Nu Stadium.

Casemiro made more than 120 appearances for Manchester United, winning the Carabao Cup and FA Cup during his time at Old Trafford. While his impact won't be measured in goals, his ability to control games, break up attacks and lead by example could prove just as valuable as Miami chase more silverware.

One of the biggest headlines as we return to the MLS season was Chicago's signing of Robert Lewandowski from Barcelona. The 37-year-old is the latest to come to America as a blockbuster transfer, hoping to help the Fire rise from third to first.

Lewandowski was denied a debut against Thomas Müller's Whitecaps due to smoky weather conditions, so it remains to be seen how he will kick off this new chapter.

He scored 14 goals from 31 appearances for the Blaugrana last season and walked away with a stunning record of 120 in 193. Though it's not really about how many he'll score for Chicago, rather, it's when. Everyone will be on high alert to watch his first hit the back of the net.

One of the youngsters who impressed in the first half of the season was Kevin Kelsy of the Portland Timbers. And he's already back up and running after the restart!

At just 21 years old, the Venezuelan centre-forward is impressing at the club, having scored 26% of their overall goals this season. He netted twice against Seattle Sounders, the first a looping header and the second a quick reaction to poke the ball home after crashing the box.

The brace sees him lead Portland's scoring charts this season, and after impressing against a rival, we're sure he will be flowing with confidence in the second half showing.

📸 Shaun Botterill - 2026 Getty Images

Naturally, how can we not mention Lionel Messi? The Argentina captain went all the way to the 2026 World Cup final while staying in contention for the Golden Boot. His ever-reliable presence for the national team is something we expect to continue for Inter Miami.

The Herons sit in second place in the Eastern Conference, largely thanks to Messi's brilliance. He already has 12 goals and seven assists after only 14 appearances this season.

That said, it will be interesting to see whether the 39-year-old experiences any fatigue as he re-enters the regular season. World Cup players are often given deserved breaks, and if Miami allows Messi to take a temporary vacation, who will step up in his absence? Without his impact, will the Herons struggle to fight for first?

A second headline signing heading into the back half of the season is Antoine Griezmann joining Orlando City. The Frenchman arrives in the United States after an impressive final season in Spain, where he registered 14 goals and eight assists across all competitions.

The Lions will look to the 35-year-old's storied experience to help lift them up from 13th in the table after just four wins so far. That poor form sees the club sit third last in the Eastern Conference.

That said, Griezmann has said he's prepared to be a leader for Orlando. "I want to win the championship, score goals, provide assists, encourage kids to play football and make them Orlando City fans," he said. "I came for all of this: I want to take Orlando City to the top of football in the United States."

📸 Dustin Satloff - 2026 Getty Images

Another youngster with his name in lights during the first half of the season was Julian Hall of the New York Red Bulls. And he's perhaps the most talked-about teenager currently in MLS.

The 18-year-old has a stunning 13 goal contributions (nine goals and four assists) from just 15 appearances. Add to that, there are also three other goals from two U.S Open Cup showings. Such numbers look like that of a veteran centre forward, rather than a high-school graduate.

After feeling refreshed from the break, it's time to see whether or not he will continue generating such hype.

After an early World Cup exit, Son Heung-min appears to be back and ready to put his best foot forward with LAFC.

The 34-year-old was a staple creative presence for the club prior to the international break, registering nine assists to help them sit third in West. That includes a statement showing against Orlando, where he produced five alone!

Now, however, Son appears hungry for goals. He scored his first of the season during the first game back against rivals LA Galaxy. Perhaps an early elimination from the World Cup and some rest was just what he needed?

📸 Alex Slitz - 2026 Getty Images

After an impressive run to the Round of 16 with Canada, defender Richie Laryea will be a player with the weight of BMO Field on his shoulders.

The veteran right-back demonstrated his veteran persona at the World Cup by playing a full 90 minutes in almost every one of Canada's games. A five-game starter, the earliest he was ever substituted off was the 78th minute.

TFC's injury issues before the break have left them struggling in 12th place in the East, but Laryea is the voice and presence at the back who can guide the team up the standings if and when he's at his best.

Looking at his stats, he has 15 goals and 26 assists in 155 appearances across all competitions for the club. He was also selected as an MLS All-Star. Will the hometown talent rise to the occasion in the second half of the season?

title: Eric Garcia reflects on Spain World Cup win: ‘No coincidence that Ferran scored the World Cup winner’
description: Eric Garcia has revealed that his next major ambition is to win the UEFA Champions League with Barcelona after helping Spain lift the FIFA World Cup.The 25-year-old defender, one of eight Barcelona pl...
fullText:
Eric Garcia has revealed that his next major ambition is to win the UEFA Champions League with Barcelona after helping Spain lift the FIFA World Cup.

The 25-year-old defender, one of eight Barcelona players in Spain’s victorious squad, is currently enjoying a well-earned break before returning for the new season.

Speaking to COPE (h/t Mundo Deportivo), Garcia reflected on the World Cup triumph, praised teammate Ferran Torres and looked ahead to his objectives with Barcelona.

Garcia admitted he was deeply moved by the reception the squad received during the victory celebrations and reserved special praise for Ferran Torres, whose goal secured Spain’s World Cup title.

Asked about the sports psychologist he shares with the Barcelona forward, Garcia highlighted the mental work both players have put in throughout their careers.

Spain’s hero. (Photo by Buda Mendes/Getty Images)

“For better or for worse, and I can include myself in that, both Ferran and I are used to surprises. Our job is to play football, which I think is a privilege,” he said.

“Things, as I’ve always said, can go better, they can go worse, but you always have to be there, with the right attitude. And in the end, it’s no coincidence that he scored the goal that gave us the World Cup.”

Garcia also reflected on making his World Cup debut in the tournament’s biggest match, explaining that he had remained prepared throughout the competition despite not featuring earlier.

“I’d been preparing all month in case the opportunity arose, and look, it finally came in the final. And to win it, which was everyone’s goal. We were all there to contribute, whether we played or not,” the Barcelona defender said.

“I’d always told the manager I was ready for whatever came my way,” he added.

Champions League the next goal. (Photo by Alex Caparros/Getty Images)

The defender also revealed the moment Spain began to believe the trophy was within reach, saying:

“After Enzo’s sending-off and when they took Julian off and brought on another defender.”

Having added the World Cup to an already impressive list of honours, Garcia made it clear that his focus has now shifted to European success with Barcelona.

“Yes, yes. It’s clear that in the end I can’t complain about the record I have to this day. Every player wants to win, to win titles, and that’s what we’re here for,” he stated.

Garcia also confirmed that he is due to report back for Barcelona duty on 12 August as preparations continue for the new season.
